title: Measurement principles and field verification
summary: Foundational synthesis connecting measurement science, uncertainty, traceability, field observations, verification and fitness-for-purpose decisions. The page explicitly remains an initial conceptual model pending detailed technical review and worked examples.

relationships.note: Measurement principles underpin surveying observations and their interpretation.
Measurement uncertainty and quality concepts support positioning assessment.
Measurement and uncertainty concepts underpin propagation and sensitivity methods.

title: Coordinate transformation and CRS axis order
summary: Explains coordinate reference systems, axis order, coordinate operations and a bounded point-transformation implementation using PROJ/pyproj. High-accuracy operation selection, dynamic reference-frame epochs, vertical transformations and raster or geometry reprojection remain outside the stated scope.

relationships.note: Coordinate operations depend on geodetic reference-system definitions.
The lesson contributes to CRS selection, transformation and coordinate QA.

title: Geodetic coordinates, ECEF and the local ENU frame
summary: Explains the transformation chain from geodetic coordinates to Earth-Centred Earth-Fixed coordinates and a local East-North-Up frame, including the distinction between ellipsoid-normal Up and geocentric radial direction.

relationships.note: The coordinate frames rely on geodetic reference and ellipsoid definitions.
Local frames support field control and local engineering measurement contexts.

title: Helmert seven-parameter transformation in geocentric coordinates
summary: Describes a seven-parameter geocentric transformation using the Position Vector convention, including parameter units and the distinction from the Coordinate Frame convention. Parameter convention and transformation scope must remain explicit.

relationships.note: The transformation relates geocentric reference frames.
This is one geodetic computation method within the broader coordinate-transformation subject.

title: Uncertainty propagation and sensitivity implementation
summary: Documents dependency-free Python baselines for positional RMSE, Monte Carlo propagation under independent uniform inputs and first-/total-order Sobol sensitivity estimates. The package states important limitations including independent uniform inputs and no arbitrary correlated input distributions.

relationships.note: The package implements selected uncertainty propagation and sensitivity baselines.
Its interpretation depends on measurement and uncertainty concepts.

title: Classification, regression, retrieval and calibration metrics implementation
summary: Documents dependency-free metrics for classification, regression, retrieval and calibration, while explicitly excluding design-based area-adjusted accuracy and other specialised estimators. Pixel-count metrics must not be misrepresented as area-adjusted estimates where the sampling design requires weighting.

relationships.note: The package provides selected metrics used in spatial quality and accuracy assessment.

title: Measurement models and measurand definition
summary: Introduces operational measurand definition and measurement models, then develops a synthetic rectangular-area example showing first-order uncertainty propagation with and without correlated inputs. It is an educational module, not a field procedure or instrument specification.

relationships.note: A focused module within the broader measurement principles and field verification foundation.
Establishes the measurement model before uncertainty evaluation.
The worked example introduces covariance-aware propagation concepts.

title: Standard uncertainty: Type A and Type B evaluation
summary: Explains Type A and Type B as methods of evaluating standard uncertainty, covers repeated-observation statistics and distribution-based Type B evaluation, and combines components using a synthetic surveying distance budget with explicit assumptions and limitations.

relationships.note: A focused uncertainty-evaluation module within the broader measurement foundation.
Uses the measurement-model and measurand definitions established in the preceding module.
Connects uncertainty evaluation to the repository's uncertainty propagation implementation.

title: Covariance, correlated observations and generalized least squares
summary: Explains covariance and correlation, covariance matrices, shared observation errors, first-order propagation with correlated inputs and generalized least-squares adjustment. It uses the repository's synthetic Exercises D and K and does not prescribe a universal field covariance model.

relationships.note: A focused stochastic-modelling module within the broader measurement foundation.
Uses measurement models and input-quantity relationships.
Builds on standard uncertainty evaluation and combination.
Connects covariance-aware uncertainty propagation to the broader uncertainty-methods subject.

title: Covariance and generalized least-squares Python implementation
summary: Provides dependency-free covariance validation, session-common covariance construction, Cholesky-based unconstrained GLS and exact-constraint GLS using a KKT system. Includes tests and synthetic Exercise D and E examples. Both solvers require positive-definite observation covariance; constrained GLS additionally requires exact constraints that remove all datum defects. Singular-covariance generalized-inverse methods remain outside scope.

relationships.note: Implements covariance validation and covariance-aware linear uncertainty adjustment.
Implements the covariance and GLS concepts developed in the foundation module.
Builds on standard uncertainty and stochastic-model concepts.

title: Exact-constraint generalized least-squares Python implementation
summary: Extends the covariance/GLS implementation with exact linear constraints solved through a Lagrange-multiplier KKT system. A rank-deficient design can be handled when constraints remove all datum defects; observation covariance must still be positive definite. Includes synthetic datum-defect tests and explicit limitations.

relationships.note: Adds exact constraints to the existing covariance and GLS implementation.
Implements a constrained least-squares adjustment for datum-deficient linear models.
Builds on the covariance and generalized least-squares foundation.

title: Mathematical language, quantities and spatial models
summary: Introduces quantities, dimensions, units, variables, equations, functions, ratios, scale, sets, discrete and continuous representations, dimensional analysis and a disciplined workflow for constructing spatial mathematical models. Examples are illustrative and distinguish mathematical relationships from assumptions about real-world data and reference systems.

relationships.note: Opening module in the mathematics for spatial science foundation domain.
Introduces vector and matrix language that is developed formally in linear algebra.
Introduces functions and relationships developed further in calculus.
Uses coordinate reference concepts to explain why coordinates require a defined reference.

title: Number systems, arithmetic and numerical representation
summary: Explains number sets, numeral bases, arithmetic with units, rounding, truncation, quantisation, significant figures, integer and floating-point storage, coordinate precision and raster scaling. Distinguishes numerical representation from measurement accuracy and uncertainty. Detailed floating-point error analysis and numerical stability are deferred to the numerical analysis foundation.

relationships.note: Second module in the mathematics for spatial science foundation domain.
Builds on mathematical language, quantities and spatial modelling.
Introduces finite numeric representation and defers numerical analysis to this foundation domain.
Connects reporting precision and resolution to measurement uncertainty.

title: Ratios, proportions, rates and logarithms
summary: Develops ratios, proportions, percentage and percentage-point change, direct and inverse proportionality, map scale, raster cell-area relationships, temporal rates, spatial density, compound growth, logarithms and decibel ratios. Worked examples and exercises emphasise denominator choice, units, reference quantities and limitations; specialised cartographic, statistical and signal-processing treatments remain in their respective foundations.

relationships.note: Third module in the mathematics for spatial science foundation domain.
Builds on the mathematical language, quantities and spatial modelling introduced in the first module.
Uses number systems and arithmetic conventions developed in the second module.
Introduces representative fraction and scale relationships; cartographic scale theory is developed in the cartography foundation.
Introduces logarithmic ratios and dynamic-range display contexts; radiometric theory is treated separately.
Introduces decibel ratios and logarithmic transformations; signal-processing theory is treated separately.

title: Equations, inequalities and mathematical reasoning
summary: Introduces algebraic expressions, equations, identities, rearrangement, dimensional consistency, linear and quadratic equations, systems, inequalities, absolute-value distance conditions, constraints, feasible sets and solution verification. Spatial examples illustrate threshold screening and distance models while distinguishing mathematical feasibility from real-world suitability. Matrix methods, advanced optimisation and geodetic distance computation remain outside scope.

relationships.note: Fourth module in the mathematics for spatial science foundation domain.
Uses the variable, quantity, unit and model language introduced in the first module.
Builds on proportional relationships and mathematical modelling conventions.
Uses a circle and coordinate-axis intersection as an introductory geometric equation.
Highlights the need for an appropriate coordinate reference and distance model when applying spatial thresholds.
Connects numerical thresholds to measurement interpretation and uncertainty without treating a stipulated cutoff as a guarantee.

title: Functions and relationships in spatial science
summary: Defines functions through domains, codomains and ranges; develops common function types, injectivity, surjectivity, inverses and composition. Spatial examples include map scale, terrain surfaces, distance functions and coordinate mappings. Distinguishes deterministic, stochastic and empirical relationships and explains model-domain, unit, interpolation and extrapolation limitations.

relationships.note: Fifth module in the mathematics for spatial science foundation domain.
Uses mathematical quantities, variables and spatial modelling language introduced in the first module.
Builds on equations and mathematical reasoning for evaluating and inverting function relationships.
Introduces coordinate mappings while reserving matrix transformations for the linear algebra foundation.
Introduces multivariable spatial functions while reserving derivatives and continuous change for calculus.
Uses geometric loci and Euclidean distance functions.
Frames coordinate reference transformations as mappings and distinguishes them from physical movement.
Distinguishes deterministic mappings from observation models and stochastic components.

title: Coordinate geometry and reference frames for spatial science
summary: Develops Cartesian coordinates, planar and three-dimensional distance, midpoints, lines, intersections, circles, planes, geometric loci and simple local-frame translations. Explains why coordinate tuples require frame, units and CRS metadata, and distinguishes planar Cartesian calculations from geographic coordinates and Earth-surface distance. Detailed geodesy, matrix transformations and numerical robustness are reserved for their dedicated foundations.

relationships.note: Sixth module in the mathematics for spatial science foundation domain.
Builds on functions and mappings to describe coordinate-based geometric relationships.
Introduces coordinate-frame changes while reserving matrix representations and rotations for linear algebra.
Introduces lines, planes, circles, distances and geometric loci.
Explains the distinction between Cartesian coordinates, geographic coordinates and geodetic reference systems.
Notes that map projections distort geometric properties and that planar map measurements require projection-aware interpretation.
Connects coordinate-derived geometry to input measurement quality and uncertainty.
Identifies finite precision, rounding and geometric numerical robustness as separate numerical-analysis concerns.

title: Vectors and vector operations for spatial science
summary: Introduces scalars, points and vectors; components, magnitude, displacement, addition, scalar multiplication, unit vectors, dot and cross products, projection and parametric lines. Spatial examples connect vectors to movement, directional fields, terrain and coordinate observations. Formal vector spaces, matrices and differential operators are reserved for linear algebra and calculus.

relationships.note: Seventh module in the mathematics for spatial science foundation domain.
Builds on coordinate geometry and reference frames to interpret coordinate differences and directions.
Uses function notation for spatial vector fields and terrain relationships.
Introduces vector operations while reserving abstract vector spaces and matrix representations for linear algebra.
Introduces the gradient connection while reserving differential operators for calculus.
Uses Euclidean geometry, angles, perpendicularity and areas.
Highlights the need for compatible coordinate frames when subtracting positions and representing directions.
Connects coordinate residuals and observed displacements to measurement interpretation without equating residuals with true errors.

title: Sequences, series and approximation for spatial science
summary: Introduces sequences, recursive updates, arithmetic and geometric sequences, limits, convergence, series, partial sums and elementary approximation. Spatial examples connect discretisation to raster resolution, curve approximation, iterative stopping criteria and time-stepped simulation. Distinguishes convergence from accuracy and numerical approximation from measurement uncertainty; advanced convergence and numerical stability are reserved for specialist foundations.

relationships.note: Eighth module in the mathematics for spatial science foundation domain.
Uses vector norms and spatial vector examples when introducing iterative vector estimates.
Connects sequences and limits to later calculus treatment.
Distinguishes deterministic sequences from stochastic processes.
Separates approximation error from measurement uncertainty.
Connects repeated updates and discretisation to algorithmic processes.
Introduces convergence and approximation while reserving numerical stability and error analysis for numerical analysis.
Connects spatial discretisation and representation choices to geographic information.
